newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Liberia's Taylor joins march of African strongmen.
newsitem.headline: Liberia's Taylor joins march of African strongmen.

text.p: Former warlord Charles Taylor's landslide victory in Liberia's election was a vote for peace in a nation torn apart by seven years of civil war.
"He killed my father but I'll vote for him," said one voter in a tell-tale comment during polling on July 19.
"He started all this and he's going to fix it," he added, summing up the dream of a bruised and war-weary nation.
But Taylor's victory, winning through the ballot box what he failed to achieve through the gun, also appears part of a wider trend -- the return, or re-emergence, of the African strongman.
"I think we are back with the authoritarian leader," Professor Willie Breytenbach of the African Studies Department at South Africa's Stellenbosch University said by telephone.
Taylor has never left any doubt about his own views.
"Everyone is fully aware that Liberia needs a very strong leader," he said after his fighters and their rivals devastated the centre of the capital in April and May 1996.
"If Liberians are looking for a weak leader they are not going to find one in Charles Taylor," he added.
Taylor inflicted a crushing defeat on Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, the newly returned former U.N. official and standard bearer of proponents of a civilian alternative untainted by the war.

It was a far cry from the optimism of the early 1990s democratic wave that broke over the continent in the wake of collapse of the Berlin Wall and the demise of Soviet communism and spawned a succession of sovereign national conferences.
Then, entrenched and established military or civilian leaders stepped aside or were forced aside by domestic and foreign pressure to make way for civilian politicians.
Today, for many of those civilian politicians, things have fallen apart, or are showing signs of doing so.

South Africa's Nelson Mandela may sometimes leave his arch rival Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi in command of the country when he and his vice-president travel. Elsewhere relations between many of Africa's leaders and their rivals are strained.
In the Congo Republic, this rivalry erupted in June into bloody ethnic and political clashes which have killed hundreds of people in the capital Brazzaville, many of them civilians.
The pre-election showdown between civilian president Pascal Lissouba and former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso has wrecked the capital of the oil-producing former French colony.
International observers gave Liberia's elections, part of a peace plan brokered by its West African neighbours, a clean bill of health.
Critics say that had Taylor lost he would have made Liberia ungovernable. Some say that had a lot to do with the result.
Taylor, 49, who plunged Liberia into civil war in December 1989, rejects suggestions he is a dictator in waiting.
"I am not going to be a wicked president," he told his victory news conference on Thursday.
His first act on winning was to offer a hand of friendship to defeated rivals. It remains to be seen on what terms.
Africa expert Richard Synge, journalist and associate of the Centre of African Studies in Cambridge, England, suggests that the national conferences were just a phase.
"Perhaps the strongman never really went away," he muses.
Stellenbosch's Breytenbach points to Gabon's veteran president, Omar Bongo, Cameroon's Paul Biya, Kenya's Daniel arap Moi as examples of this. Togo's Gnassingbe Eyadema is another.
"We already saw that under the guise of multi-party democracy, wily old leaders out-foxed their opponents at the polling booths," he said.
In former Zaire, veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko blocked effective change by playing a game of divide and rule.
Laurent Kabila toppled Mobutu in May and renamed Africa's third largest nation the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

But his first acts in power have been those of a traditional African strongman rather than a democrat. He has banned political activity and accorded himself wide-ranging powers. Elections, whether multi-party or not, remain two years away.
In black Africa's most populous nation, Nigeria, General Sani Abacha has embarked on a civilian rule programme scheduled to end in 1998. Most pundits predict he will run for office -- and win.
In neighbouring Benin, Nicephore Soglo lost to his Marxist military predecessor Mathieu Kerekou in 1996 elections -- having aliened onetime political allies with his autocratic style.
In Niger, Ibrahim Bare Mainassara toppled elected president Mahamane Ousmane in 1996 and won election as president -- after scrapping the election commission in mid-poll.
In tiny Gambia, Yahya Jammeh, toppled independence president Sir Dawda Jawara in 1994 and then won election as president.
Mali was one of the stars of the 1990s wave of democratic reform. Second time round, things have proved more difficult.
Historian Alpha Oumar Konare won reelection in May and his party notched up a landslide win on July 20 -- but the radical opposition boycotted both elections and turnout was low.
Sierra Leone was a late arrival in the multi-party stakes. Soldiers there toppled elected civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah on May 25 -- after just over a year in office.
There, the talk among the junta and its rebel allies is of a national conference. Its neighbours, led by Nigeria's Abacha, are pressing for Kabbah's return.
